name: Prize crossword No 26,687
preamble: Six solutions are characters, not further defined, from 18's work about 5 down 21 across.

blocks.note: surface reading: whoever cooks a pot of soup
setter's reading: the American brand famous for canned soup, whose name is also a surname

explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says six answers are characters from the novel with no definition of their own; this one is Alan Campbell, the chemist Dorian blackmails, clued only through the soup company.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Campbell is the scientist in Wilde's novel who is forced to dispose of the painter's body.

clue.text: Penny is very good to counter rumour

indicators.note: to counter is to run against, so the letters run against their usual direction

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for a penny
taken as written
so means very, as in 'so good'
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone praises a penny-pincher in order to scotch a whispered story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny is very good' reads as a sentence about a woman called Penny; it is four separate pieces that are then turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip and rumour are both idle talk about other people, often unconfirmed, so they are synonyms.

definitions.note: read as a noun phrase, the time spent on a call

blocks.note: first meaning: to bring something to an end, as a publican does at closing
second meaning: the minutes spent on a phone call, as on a mobile tariff

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one instruction to hang up; split it and each half is a sense of the phrase. Calling time is what a British pub landlord does at closing.
explanation.definitionFit: To call time on something is an idiom for ending it, and the phrase can also mean minutes used making calls.

clue.text: It's funny having looked over children's TV programme

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or out of the ordinary, so the letters come out in an odd order
turned over means flipped, so the word is read the other way

blocks.note: the letters of the word, apostrophe dropped
saw is the past tense of see, to look

explanation.surface: Someone reviewing a children's TV show finds it funny.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiswas was an anarchic British Saturday-morning children's show on ITV in the 1970s and early 1980s, famous for custard pies and buckets of water.
explanation.definitionFit: The name refers to a specific British Saturday-morning show for young viewers, hosted by Chris Tarrant among others.

definitions.note: the answer read as two words, a phrase meaning dressed in drag

blocks.note: first meaning: a fire-breathing monster of fable
second meaning, split into two words: wearing women's clothes, as a cross-dresser does

explanation.surface: A glamorous drag performer is described as a fabulous creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' looks like gushing praise for a performer; here it means belonging to fable. Split the answer as DRAG ON and it describes someone with their drag on.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragon is a monster of myth and legend, so it is a creature found in fables.

indicators.note: in a down entry, moving the article lower shifts it further down the word, rearranging the letters

blocks.note: to adore is to worship
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A devotee bows before a dim lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: The A of the worship word slides down the column four places, then the beam is added. The preamble names this as the subject of Oscar Wilde's novel, so it needs no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorian Gray is the title character of Wilde's only novel, whose portrait ages while he stays young.

clue.text: Endless traffic problem leads to toll

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
a problem is something gone wrong, so the letters are in a wrong order

blocks.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Constant congestion on the roads leads to a road charge being introduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traffic problem' reads as one phrase about jams; 'Endless' trims the first word and 'problem' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tariff is a charge or duty levied, and a toll is a fee paid for use of a road, so both are charges.

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters fall into a new order
one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: FR is the abbreviation for France
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is even more distressed while in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says this answer is a character from Wilde's novel and gets no definition: Lord Fermor is Lord Henry's uncle.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Fermor is the elderly uncle whom Lord Henry consults about Dorian's family background.

clue.text: Cooked tea right? It's to be seriously questioned

blocks.note: cha is slang for tea
R is the abbreviation for right
to grill someone is to interrogate them hard

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether the tea was made properly, then is told it will face hard questioning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked tea' looks like a single phrase about a meal; 'Cooked' is the definition and 'tea' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chargrilled food has been cooked over a very hot grill so that it is lightly charred.

indicators.note: less means minus, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: gorillas are an example of great apes
taken as written, and removed

explanation.surface: Gorillas, perhaps, cut back on their fruit intake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals an example: gorillas are one kind of great ape. Take the three letters of the eating word out of that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapes are small round berries grown in bunches on vines, a common kind of fruit.

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a hall is the entrance area of a house
the first four letters are the verb, and the last four are the reversal signal

explanation.surface: A doorway comes with a downside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawback' reads as one word meaning disadvantage; split it into the verb and its reversal signal. Basil Hallward is the painter of the portrait in Wilde's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Basil Hallward is the artist who paints the portrait and is later murdered by its sitter.

indicators.note: what is captured is held inside, so the letters lie within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the camera abbreviation into the particle

explanation.surface: A security camera has somehow filmed a subatomic particle.
explanation.walkthrough: Sibyl Vane is the young actress Dorian loves and abandons in Wilde's novel; the preamble supplies her, so the clue is all wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sibyl Vane is the young actress whom the hero jilts, driving her to suicide.

blocks.note: per means for each, as in 'per head'
a mission is an assigned task or piece of business

explanation.surface: A permit is required for every company.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a trading licence per company; 'Licence' is the definition, in its sense of being allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Licence in the sense of freedom to act is an authorisation, the same as being given leave.

clue.text: "Tenses up pecs" left Rita's head giddy!

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the opening letter is kept
giddy means dizzy and reeling, so the letters spin into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A gym-goer flexing their chest muscles leaves Rita feeling faint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tenses up' reads as one verb about muscles; the definition is 'Tenses' as a grammar noun, and the rest is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The pluperfect is the past perfect form of a verb, as in 'had gone', so plural forms are grammatical tenses.

blocks.note: first meaning: strong, having great force
second meaning: having a strong effect

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like one phrase, an intensifier and adjective; each is a separate sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both great physical strength and a strong effect on the senses or emotions.

blocks.note: surface reading: the principal tall buildings of a place
setter's reading: vessels that tow ships across the main, an old word for the sea

explanation.walkthrough: 'Towers' rhymes with 'flowers' here, not 'powers': things that tow. The main is a poetic word for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Small powerful harbour vessels pull larger ships, so they haul things at sea.

clue.text: Guard caught stealing gold after drugs

indicators.note: to steal is to take something in, so one piece holds the other
coming after means placed later in the line

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so drugs are Es
ct is a scorecard abbreviation for caught
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A security guard is arrested for stealing gold after a drugs offence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a crime report; 'caught stealing' is the abbreviation taking in the heraldic metal.
explanation.definitionFit: An escort accompanies someone to protect them, so as a verb or noun it means a guard.

clue.text: It's mostly hiding in red wine

definitions.text: It's mostly hiding in red wine

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a hiding is a beating, also called a tanning; drop the end

explanation.surface: Something lurks inside a glass of red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiding' looks like concealment, but it is a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tannin is the astringent compound from grape skins that gives red wine its drying taste.

clue.text: O, much wit, then led astray?

definitions.text: O, much wit, then led astray?

indicators.note: much of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter goes
astray means wandering off course, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the word without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a famously witty man who was then led into scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the writer: celebrated for his wit, then 'led astray' into the affair that ruined him. 'O' is the radio-alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde was the great Victorian wit whose relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas led to his imprisonment and disgrace.

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective meaning standing in, not an infinitive

blocks.note: first meaning: putting on a performance, feigning
second meaning: serving temporarily in someone's place

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about faking a substitution; it splits into two separate senses of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting is both performing a pretence and holding a post temporarily on behalf of someone absent.

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something turns it upward, so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: eg, for example, is what 'say' means in 'fruit, say'
a gong is slang for a medal or award

explanation.surface: A celebratory drink as a team raises the cup.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters of 'on' already sit inside the award word; flip just those. A gong is British slang for a medal or honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a sweet drink of eggs, milk and sugar, often with rum or brandy, popular at Christmas.

clue.text: Change key after party rejected music

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came

blocks.note: Con is short for the Conservative Party
to turn is to change, as milk turns
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: A band changes key after their party snubbed the music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change key' looks like a single musical instruction; the two words are separate pieces. Con is the abbreviation for Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A nocturne is a dreamy piece of music evoking the night, as written by Chopin.

clue.text: Arsenal's French striker misses one, takes new position

indicators.note: to miss something is to leave it out
to take in is to hold, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: Olivier Giroud, French centre forward for Arsenal at the time
I is the Roman numeral one
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A football report: Arsenal's French forward fluffs a chance and moves to a new spot on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Arsenal is a London football club and Olivier Giroud was its French striker. 'Misses one' looks like a missed shot, but it removes the numeral; 'position' is the definition, not part of the match report.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground means a stance or point of view, as in 'stand your ground' or 'common ground'.

indicators.note: a disguise covers something up, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: tone is an accent or manner of voice
G is the abbreviation for government
U means upper-class, from the 1950s U and non-U usage debate

explanation.surface: A put-on accent hides how plummy the government's speech really is.
explanation.walkthrough: U as 'upper-class' comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, a British label for posh speech habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue is an old or literary word for a language, as in 'mother tongue' or 'speaking in tongues'.

blocks.note: w is the abbreviation for with
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books
a ton is slang for a hundred

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: posh language comes with books bought in their hundreds.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the clue before, but this answer stands alone: Lord Henry Wotton, the cynical aristocrat who corrupts Dorian.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Henry Wotton is the epigram-spouting aristocrat whose ideas lead the hero astray in Wilde's novel.
